definition: A documented history of who collected, held, transferred, and stored an item of evidence.
wrongs: A hash of a file that replaces the need to record any custodian.
A software license that lets an examiner copy any disk without notes.
A network route showing which routers forwarded a packet.
why: Courts and reviewers use that history to judge whether the evidence stayed accounted for.
example: Each time a seized laptop moves from the scene officer to the lab locker, both people sign the transfer record.
scenario: A seized phone changes hands three times before analysis. Which record shows who held it at each step?
scenarioWhy: The chain of custody is the ongoing record of each person who had the phone.

definition: A forensically acquired copy of digital media, preserved so the original can stay unchanged.
wrongs: A screenshot of the desktop that replaces a copy of the disk.
A photograph of the outside of a computer case.
A list of file names typed from memory after the disk is returned.
why: The image lets examiners work from a verified copy while the source media is protected.
example: The lab copies a seized drive to an image file, checks its hash, and stores the original drive in a locker.
scenario: Examiners need a complete copy of a drive for analysis while the seized drive stays sealed. What should they create?
scenarioWrongs: A photo of the drive label
scenarioWhy: A forensic image is the working copy of the media, verified and kept separate from the original.

definition: Hardware or software that lets an examiner read source media while blocking write commands to it.
wrongs: A tool that speeds up a disk by caching writes onto the evidence drive.
A program that encrypts the examiner's notes before they are saved.
A filter that hides file names during a keyword search.
why: Blocking writes protects the original evidence from changes made by the examination computer.
example: An examiner connects a seized drive through a hardware write blocker and confirms the operating system cannot save files to it.
scenario: A seized disk must be read on a lab computer without that computer altering the disk. What device should sit between them?
scenarioWrongs: A disk duplicator set to overwrite the source
An ordinary USB hub with no write protection
scenarioWhy: A write blocker permits reading the evidence disk and stops the lab computer from writing to it.

definition: Recovering file contents from raw stored bytes by matching file-structure patterns when directory entries are missing.
wrongs: Copying only the files that currently appear in a normal folder listing.
Compressing a forensic report so it fits in an email.
Renaming evidence files so their extensions match their hashes.
why: Carving uses internal file patterns, so it can find files whose file-system metadata is gone.
example: After a directory entry is missing, the lab recovers a photo by finding its header pattern in unallocated space.
scenario: Directory entries for deleted pictures are gone, but the picture bytes may remain on the disk. Which method looks for those bytes by file structure?
scenarioWrongs: Reading only the current folder listing
scenarioWhy: File carving searches raw data for known file patterns when the directory no longer points to the files.

definition: A recorded date and time tied to an event or to a file action such as creation or modification.
wrongs: The hash of a file's contents, which does not record when anything happened.
The serial number printed on the outside of a disk.
The name of the examiner who later opened a report.
why: Timestamps are the file system's or log's recorded times, which a timeline can place in order.
example: A document's modified time shows 14:02, and examiners compare that time with the server log for the same minute.
scenario: Investigators want the recorded modification time of a report file, not a hash of its text. Which value do they read?
scenarioWhy: A timestamp is the stored date and time associated with the file action.

definition: Memory whose contents disappear when power is removed, including registers and RAM.
wrongs: A hard disk that keeps files after the computer is unplugged.
An archival tape stored in an evidence locker.
A printed log placed in the case folder.
why: Volatile contents exist only while the system has power, so they are collected before shutdown when they matter.
example: A running server holds active network connections in RAM that will vanish if the server loses power.
scenario: A running workstation will be unplugged. Which evidence is most likely to disappear when the power goes off?
scenarioWrongs: Files already stored on the hard disk
A tape stored in the evidence room
scenarioWhy: RAM is volatile memory, so its contents are lost when power is removed.

definition: A system record of notable activity such as logons, service errors, or process starts.
wrongs: A photograph of the desk where a computer was found.
A hash computed over an entire disk image.
A warrant that authorizes a search of one office.
why: Event logs store time-stamped activity that can be correlated with other artifacts.
example: A Windows security log shows a successful logon for a lab account at 09:14 on the exam morning.
scenario: An examiner needs the recorded logon times for an account on a server. Which artifact is the usual source?
scenarioWhy: Event logs are the system's own record of activities such as account logons.

definition: A structured document that states the examiner's methods, findings, limitations, and conclusions.
wrongs: A raw disk image with no description of methods or results.
An unsigned sticky note that only says the case is finished.
A vendor advertisement for a forensic tool.
why: The report is how findings, limits, and the process used are communicated to other reviewers.
example: The lab report lists the image hash, the tools and versions used, three findings, and one limitation about a bad sector.
scenario: Counsel asks for the methods, hashes, findings, and limits of an examination in one document. What should the examiner provide?
scenarioWrongs: An unlabeled screenshot with no notes
scenarioWhy: A forensic report brings together the methods, evidence identifiers, findings, and limitations.

definition: The legal fitness of evidence or expert testimony to be considered by a court.
wrongs: The speed at which a forensic tool finishes a keyword search.
The compression ratio of a stored disk image.
The font size used on an evidence label.
why: Admissibility depends on rules about relevance, reliability, and lawful collection, not on tool speed.
example: A judge considers whether a drive image was lawfully seized and whether the lab process is reliable enough to present.
scenario: A judge must decide whether a drive image and the examiner's testimony may be considered at trial. What quality is being decided?
scenarioWhy: Admissibility is the court's decision about whether that evidence may be considered.

definition: The practice of collecting the most short-lived evidence before evidence that persists longer.
wrongs: The practice of imaging archival tapes before looking at a running system's memory.
The practice of labeling bags only after the case is closed.
The practice of hashing paper notes before photographing the screen.
why: Evidence such as RAM can vanish quickly, while data on a powered-down disk remains longer.
example: At a live server, responders capture memory before they image the hard disk and long before they box the backup tapes.
scenario: A server is still running, and both RAM and the hard disk matter. Which source should be collected first?
scenarioWrongs: The spare drives still in sealed boxes
scenarioWhy: Order of volatility puts the short-lived RAM contents ahead of data that will still be on disk.

definition: Comparing a newly computed cryptographic hash with an earlier hash to show a copy still matches.
wrongs: Changing file contents until their hash equals a chosen value.
Deleting a log because its hash was already written down.
Replacing the original disk with the examiner's notebook.
why: If the hashes match, the copied bits are the same as the bits hashed at acquisition.
example: After imaging, the lab hashes the image again and checks that it equals the hash recorded when the drive was acquired.
scenario: An image was hashed at acquisition, and the lab hashes it again before trial. What does a match support?
scenarioAnswer: The image is unchanged since acquisition
scenarioWrongs: The clock was set to universal time
scenarioWhy: Matching hashes show the image bits are the same as when the acquisition hash was made.

definition: The duplicate that examiners analyze so the original evidence media can remain unchanged.
wrongs: The seized original disk that is mounted for everyday editing.
A blank drive that has not yet received any image.
A public web page describing the case in general terms.
why: Analysis belongs on the duplicate so routine examination does not alter the source.
example: Examiners search a restored copy of the image on a lab drive and leave the seized disk in sealed storage.
scenario: Keyword searches should not be run on the sealed original disk. What should the examiner search instead?
scenarioWhy: The working copy is the duplicate reserved for analysis while the original stays protected.

definition: The source device or storage received as evidence, as distinct from copies made from it.
wrongs: The lab computer used only to write the final report.
A blank drive bought to hold an image.
A photocopy of the examiner's notes.
why: The original is the source item whose condition and custody must be preserved.
example: The seized laptop drive stays in a sealed bag, while all searching is done on an image made from it.
scenario: A bag labeled as evidence contains the drive taken from the scene, not the lab's later copy. What is that drive?
scenarioWhy: Original media is the source item collected as evidence, before laboratory copies are made.

definition: Disk areas not currently assigned to an active file, which may still hold remnants of deleted data.
wrongs: The space inside a file that the application is currently editing.
The paper margin on a printed forensic report.
The empty shelf space in an evidence locker.
why: Deleting a file often removes its directory entry while leaving bytes in clusters that are no longer allocated.
example: A picture no longer appears in any folder, but its bytes are still found in unallocated clusters on the image.
scenario: A user deleted a document and emptied the trash, yet remnants may remain outside any active file. Where do examiners look?
scenarioWrongs: The BIOS setup screen's help text
scenarioWhy: Unallocated space can retain data from files that are no longer assigned a directory entry.

definition: Leftover bytes in a file's last allocated unit that are not part of that file's current contents.
wrongs: The free space of an entire empty partition.
The unused lines at the end of a written report.
The gap between two computers on a shelf.
why: Storage is allocated in units larger than the file's last partial unit, so older bytes can remain in the leftover part.
example: A 100-byte text file occupies a larger cluster, and the unused tail of that cluster still contains bytes from an older file.
scenario: A short file does not fill its last cluster, and older bytes remain in the unused tail. What is that unused tail called?
scenarioWhy: File slack is the unused remainder of the last allocated unit of a file.

definition: The characteristic starting bytes that identify a file type, often called a magic number.
wrongs: The alphabetic extension typed at the end of a file name.
The handwritten signature on a chain-of-custody form.
The hash of the whole disk image.
why: Many file types begin with a known byte pattern that identifies them even if the name is wrong or missing.
example: A file named notes.txt begins with the JPEG start-of-image bytes, so examiners treat it as a picture, not plain text.
scenario: A file's name ends in .txt, but examiners want the type indicated by its first bytes. What do they inspect?
scenarioWrongs: The color of the evidence bag
scenarioWhy: The header signature is the leading byte pattern that identifies the file type.

definition: Data about an item, such as its size, owner, or timestamps, as distinct from its visible content.
wrongs: The paragraph text that a user typed inside a document.
The photograph pixels that form the picture itself.
The spoken words in an audio recording.
why: Metadata describes the item and its history, while content is what the item directly displays or plays.
example: A spreadsheet's cells are content, while its author name and last-saved time are metadata.
scenario: Examiners already have the words inside a letter and now want its author field and last-saved time. What are those fields?
scenarioWhy: Author and last-saved time describe the file, so they are metadata rather than the letter's wording.

definition: Placing digital events and recorded file times into chronological order to reconstruct activity.
wrongs: Sorting files only by name and ignoring when anything occurred.
Computing one hash for an entire case folder.
Listing every tool the lab owns, without reference to the case.
why: A timeline shows sequence, which helps relate logs, file times, and other artifacts.
example: The lab orders a USB connection record, a document's modified time, and a logoff event from the same afternoon.
scenario: An examiner wants to see whether a file change happened before or after a logon on the same computer. Which method helps?
scenarioWrongs: Counting the pages in the warrant
scenarioWhy: Timeline analysis puts the file time and the logon into one chronological sequence.

definition: Collecting evidence from a system that is still powered on, including memory and running state.
wrongs: Imaging a drive only after the computer has been shut down and unplugged.
Photographing a sealed bag days after the device left the scene.
Copying files from a backup tape stored offline.
why: A powered-on system still holds volatile state that a later shutdown would lose.
example: Responders capture the RAM and active connection list of a server before anyone powers it down.
scenario: Encrypted containers are open only while a server stays on, and memory may hold useful state. Which collection approach fits?
scenarioWrongs: Waiting to image a cold backup tape only
scenarioWhy: Live acquisition collects evidence while the system is still running and that state still exists.

definition: Imaging storage after the system has been powered down, so the drive is copied in a stable state.
wrongs: Capturing RAM while the operating system is still running.
Recording the screen of an active video call.
Exporting a process list from a live operating system.
why: With the system off, the storage is not being changed by a running operating system during the copy.
example: The lab removes a powered-off laptop disk, connects it through a write blocker, and images it.
scenario: A desktop is already off, and the team needs a stable copy of its drive rather than RAM. Which acquisition fits?
scenarioWrongs: A memory dump from the running desktop
A photograph of the login screen
A copy of the examiner's live notes only
scenarioWhy: Dead acquisition images stable storage from a system that is not running.

definition: A tamper-evident closure on evidence packaging so later opening can be detected.
wrongs: A password used to log in to the examiner's workstation.
A hash stored in the forensic report.
A software lock on a case-management program.
why: A broken or replaced seal shows that the package may have been opened after it was closed.
example: The evidence bag's numbered seal is intact when the drive reaches the lab, matching the number on the intake form.
scenario: A drive arrives with its bag closure cut and replaced by an unnumbered strip. What was supposed to show that change?
scenarioWhy: An evidence seal is meant to make opening the package detectable.

definition: The quality of a method that preserves original evidence and can be documented and reviewed.
wrongs: The quality of finishing an exam as quickly as possible with no notes.
The quality of editing original files so they open faster.
The quality of a report's visual design.
why: A sound process avoids changing the original and leaves enough documentation for another expert to review.
example: The lab uses a tested write blocker, records hashes, and notes every step so another examiner can review the process.
scenario: A procedure never alters the original disk and records enough detail for another expert to review it. Which quality does it have?
scenarioWhy: Forensic soundness means the original is preserved and the method can be reviewed.

definition: A forensic tool whose output has been tested against known inputs and expected results.
wrongs: Any newly downloaded utility that has never been checked on known data.
A word processor used only to type the report title.
A camera that has not been tested because it is new.
why: Validation shows that, for the tested tasks, the tool produces results that match known ground truth.
example: Before casework, the lab runs a carving tool on a test image with known files and compares the recovered set with the answer key.
scenario: A lab wants evidence that its imaging program copies a test disk correctly before using it in cases. What should that program be?
scenarioWrongs: An untested utility from an unknown site
A game used to stress the CPU
scenarioWhy: A validated tool has been tested on known data and produced the expected results.

definition: The ability of a qualified examiner, following the documented process, to reach the same result.
wrongs: The ability to obtain a different result each time the same image is examined.
The ability to skip notes because the first examiner remembers the steps.
The ability to change the original so the result is easier to see.
why: If the data and the documented method stay the same, another examiner should be able to reproduce the result.
example: A second examiner repeats the documented hash check on the same image and gets the same digest.
scenario: Another qualified examiner follows the written steps on the same image and gets the same hash. Which property is that?
scenarioWrongs: A result that changes on every run
Editing the original until the hash matches
scenarioWhy: Repeatability means the documented process produces the same result when it is followed again.

definition: A comparison of file hashes with a library of known-good or known-bad files so examiners can prioritize the rest.
wrongs: A spelling check of the forensic report.
A filter that hides every file larger than one kilobyte.
A sort that groups files only by their color icons.
why: Matching a known hash lets examiners set aside standard files or highlight files already identified as notable.
example: The lab ignores thousands of standard operating-system files whose hashes match a known-good library and reviews the remaining files.
scenario: Most files on a system disk are ordinary operating-system files. How can hashes help the examiner focus on the others?
scenarioAnswer: Compare them with a known-file library
scenarioWrongs: Delete every file whose name is short
Ignore hashes and open files at random
scenarioWhy: A known-file filter uses hashes to separate familiar library files from the files that still need review.

definition: A captured copy of volatile memory contents, saved so they can be examined later.
wrongs: A sector copy of a powered-off hard disk.
A paper printout of a chain-of-custody form.
A photograph of a computer's serial-number sticker.
why: The dump preserves RAM contents that would otherwise disappear when the machine powers off.
example: Responders save a server's RAM to an external drive and later review the processes that were in memory.
scenario: Analysts need to study the processes that were in RAM after the server has been shut down. What must already have been saved?
scenarioWrongs: A photograph of the server front panel
A copy of the paper warranty
An image of a spare blank disk
scenarioWhy: A memory dump is the saved copy of RAM that can be examined after the live state is gone.

definition: Attaching a file system so it can be viewed without writing changes back to that file system.
wrongs: Opening a disk so the operating system may update access times and journals on it.
Formatting the evidence disk before searching it.
Copying the examiner's notes onto the seized drive.
why: A read-only mount is one control, often used with a write blocker, to avoid changing the examined copy.
example: The lab mounts an image read-only so browsing folders does not update timestamps on that image.
scenario: An examiner must browse an image without the operating system writing timestamps back to it. How should it be mounted?
scenarioWrongs: Read-write with journaling enabled on the evidence
As a drive that stores the examiner's notes
scenarioWhy: A read-only mount lets the examiner view the file system without writing changes to it.

definition: A sector-by-sector copy of storage that includes active files, slack, and unallocated space.
wrongs: A copy of only the files currently visible in folders.
A typed list of file names without their contents.
A compressed summary that keeps headings but drops file bytes.
why: Copying every sector preserves remnants that a normal file-by-file copy would skip.
example: The imaging program copies every sector of a laptop disk, including clusters not assigned to any current file.
scenario: Deleted-file remnants in unallocated space must be included in the copy. Which copy type does that?
scenarioWrongs: A copy of visible files only
A backup of the examiner's email
scenarioWhy: A bit-stream copy takes every sector, so unallocated space is included.

definition: A copy of data visible through the file system, which does not include unallocated space.
wrongs: A sector-by-sector image that includes slack and unallocated space.
A capture of CPU registers and RAM.
A photograph of the physical device only.
why: Logical acquisition follows the file system, so deleted remnants outside active files are left behind.
example: A phone extraction copies the visible photo library and messages but not leftover bytes from deleted items.
scenario: A copy includes current messages and photos but misses deleted data outside the file system. Which acquisition is that?
scenarioWhy: Logical acquisition copies file-system-visible data and omits unallocated remnants.

definition: Target media that has been wiped and checked before an image is written, so old data cannot mix in.
wrongs: A used drive that still contains another case's files.
The seized source disk that is about to be imaged.
A folder of the examiner's personal photographs.
why: Wiping and verifying the destination prevents leftover bytes from being mistaken for evidence.
example: Before imaging, the lab wipes the target drive and confirms the wipe so case data will be the only content written.
scenario: A destination drive previously held another case. What must it be before a new image is written?
scenarioWrongs: Left full of the previous case
Replaced by the seized source disk
Used as the examiner's personal backup
scenarioWhy: Sterile destination media has been wiped and checked so previous data cannot mix with the new image.

definition: The difference between a device clock and a trusted reference time.
wrongs: The hash difference between two identical copies of a file.
The physical distance between two evidence lockers.
The number of pages in a forensic report.
why: If the device clock is fast or slow, its timestamps must be interpreted against a known reference.
example: A camera clock is 12 minutes fast compared with a trusted time source, so photo times are adjusted in the timeline notes.
scenario: A laptop clock is 20 minutes behind a trusted source. What is that 20-minute difference called?
scenarioWhy: Clock skew is the offset between the laptop clock and the trusted reference time.

definition: The idea that contact or interaction leaves traces that a later examination may detect.
wrongs: The idea that digital actions leave no artifacts of any kind.
The idea that only paper documents can be evidence.
The idea that hashes replace the need to look for traces.
why: Digital actions such as connecting a device or opening a file often leave artifacts elsewhere on the system.
example: Connecting a removable drive leaves records on the computer even after the drive itself is unplugged.
scenario: A removable drive was connected and then removed. Which principle explains why the computer may still hold traces of that connection?
scenarioWrongs: The claim that use leaves no traces
The rule that only paper is evidence
The idea that a hash erases history
scenarioWhy: Locard's exchange principle says the interaction can leave detectable traces on the computer.

definition: An instruction to preserve information that may be relevant because a legal matter is expected or underway.
wrongs: A request to delete logs once a complaint is received.
A tool setting that compresses images by discarding sectors.
A note that tells staff to reuse sterilized drives for personal files.
why: A legal hold suspends ordinary deletion so potentially relevant information remains available.
example: After counsel issues a hold, the university stops its usual deletion of the relevant mailbox and server logs.
scenario: A lawsuit is anticipated, and routine deletion would remove relevant mail. What instruction should management issue first?
scenarioWrongs: An order to delete the mailboxes
A request to format the log server
A note to pause all backups forever without preserving anything
scenarioWhy: A legal hold directs staff to preserve information that may be relevant to the matter.

definition: The destruction or material alteration of evidence that should have been preserved for a legal process.
wrongs: The careful imaging of a drive onto sterile media.
The signing of a chain-of-custody form.
The writing of contemporaneous examination notes.
why: Once a duty to preserve exists, destroying or materially changing that evidence is spoliation.
example: Staff wipe a relevant server after a preservation notice, and the court later treats that wiping as spoliation.
scenario: Relevant logs are wiped after a preservation duty has begun. What is that destruction called?
scenarioWhy: Spoliation is the improper destruction or material alteration of evidence that should have been kept.

definition: The person who first secures a digital scene and begins preservation before a full laboratory examination.
wrongs: The judge who later rules on admissibility.
The vendor that sold the imaging software.
The juror who reads the final report.
why: Early scene control reduces the chance that evidence will be lost, altered, or undocumented.
example: The on-call staff member isolates a running lab computer, photographs the screen, and records who is present before the drive is imaged.
scenario: Someone must secure a live computer and start preservation before the full lab exam begins. Which role is that?
scenarioWhy: The first responder is responsible for the initial securing and preservation of the scene.

definition: Packaging built so that opening or altering it leaves a visible sign.
wrongs: A reusable grocery bag with no closure record.
An unsealed cardboard box used for convenience.
A clear sleeve that can be opened and resealed without any mark.
why: Visible damage to the packaging warns custodians that the contents may have been accessed.
example: A numbered evidence bag shows a broken seal strip, so intake staff document that the packaging was opened.
scenario: Storage materials should make it obvious if someone opens a bag after it leaves the scene. What kind of packaging is required?
scenarioWrongs: A sleeve that reseals without a mark
scenarioWhy: Tamper-evident packaging is designed to show a visible sign if it is opened.

definition: Notes written at the time of an action, recording what was done, when, and by whom.
wrongs: A summary typed months later from memory with no dates.
A vendor manual that was never marked for the case.
A calendar invitation that only says a meeting exists.
why: Notes made at the time are more reliable than a reconstruction written long afterward.
example: While imaging, the examiner writes the start time, tool version, and drive identifier in the case notebook.
scenario: Months later, nobody remembers the imaging start time. Which record should already contain it because it was written during the work?
scenarioWhy: Contemporaneous notes are made while the action happens, so the start time would be recorded then.

definition: The legal limit on which devices, data, places, or time periods an examiner may search.
wrongs: The maximum speed of the laboratory's imaging computer.
The font limit in the report template.
The shelf height of the evidence locker.
why: Authority such as a warrant or consent defines the boundaries of a lawful examination.
example: A warrant covers one office desktop, so the examiner does not image personal phones that the warrant does not include.
scenario: A warrant names one desktop and not the employees' phones. What sets that limit on the examination?
scenarioWrongs: The speed of the imaging PC
The size of the evidence room
scenarioWhy: The scope of authority is the legal boundary on what may be searched.

definition: Sending event records to another host so a later local change does not erase the only copy.
wrongs: Keeping the only log copy in memory on the same machine being investigated.
Printing logs and then shredding both the paper and the file.
Disabling logs whenever a disk becomes half full.
why: A copy on another host can survive clearing or failure of the local log.
example: A firewall sends its logs to a separate server, which still has them after the firewall's local buffer is cleared.
scenario: Investigators need firewall events from last week, but the firewall's local buffer was cleared yesterday. Which practice would have kept a copy?
scenarioWrongs: Storing the only copy in the firewall's memory
Disabling logging when the disk filled
Deleting the log server each night
scenarioWhy: Remote logging places a copy on another host that can survive clearing of the local buffer.

definition: A standard format and service for sending device event messages to a logging host.
wrongs: A file system used to store photographs on camera cards.
A court standard for qualifying expert witnesses.
A hash algorithm used only for disk images.
why: Syslog gives devices a common way to forward event messages to a collector.
example: A network switch forwards authentication events to a campus syslog server that retains them after the switch reboots.
scenario: A switch can only keep a short local event buffer. Which standard service can forward those events to a logging server?
scenarioWhy: Syslog is the standard service used to send device events to a logging host.

definition: Metadata stored inside a photo file, which can include camera details and the capture time.
wrongs: The visible pixels that make up the picture.
A separate paper log that was never embedded in the file.
The hash of the forensic image that contains the photo.
why: EXIF is embedded metadata about the photo, not the picture pixels themselves.
example: A lawfully seized camera photo has an EXIF capture time that examiners compare with the camera's clock offset.
scenario: Examiners have a seized photo and need the capture time stored inside the file, not a hash of the disk. What do they read?
scenarioWrongs: The image hash of the whole disk
scenarioWhy: EXIF data is the embedded metadata that can store the photo's capture time.

definition: The NTFS system file that stores a record for each file, including attributes and cluster locations.
wrongs: A paper index taped to the front of an evidence locker.
The first sector of a disk that holds boot code on older PCs.
A spreadsheet the examiner creates to list exhibit numbers.
why: NTFS keeps file records in the master file table, so those records describe names, times, and locations.
example: On an NTFS image, examiners read a document's record in the master file table to see its timestamps and cluster run.
scenario: On an NTFS volume, where is the per-file record of a document's attributes and cluster locations stored?
scenarioWrongs: Only in the examiner's exhibit spreadsheet
scenarioWhy: The master file table is the NTFS structure that holds each file's record.

definition: A file-system feature that records pending changes so the system can recover after an interruption.
wrongs: A paper diary kept by the examiner after hours.
A court reporter's transcript of testimony.
A hash list printed at the end of a report.
why: The journal describes recent intended changes and can contain artifacts useful to a timeline.
example: After a power loss, an NTFS volume uses its journal to finish or undo file-system changes that were in progress.
scenario: A volume records intended file-system changes so it can recover after a crash. What is that feature called?
scenarioWhy: Journaling is the file system's own log of pending changes used for recovery.

definition: A stored browser record, often in a local database, of pages visited by a user account.
wrongs: The live web page as it exists on the public internet today.
A firewall rule that blocks one domain for the whole campus.
A paper bookmark stuck to a monitor.
why: The artifact is local stored history, which can remain after the browser window is closed.
example: The lab reads a browser database on the image and finds a record of a library page visited at 16:40.
scenario: A browser window is closed, but the account's visited pages may still be stored locally. What is that stored record?
scenarioWrongs: Today's copy of the public website
A paper note on the monitor
scenarioWhy: A browser history artifact is the local stored record of pages the account visited.

definition: The formal check-in of an item, recording its description, condition, identifiers, and receiving custodian.
wrongs: The final courtroom testimony of an expert.
The deletion of a case folder when the report is printed.
The purchase of a new imaging computer.
why: Intake starts the laboratory record of what arrived, in what condition, and who received it.
example: At the lab door, staff record the laptop's serial number, the intact seal number, and the name of the person receiving it.
scenario: A sealed laptop arrives at the lab. Which step records its serial number, condition, and the person who received it?
scenarioWhy: Evidence intake is the formal check-in that records the item, its condition, and its receiver.

definition: A laboratory setup kept off the general network so examination does not change live operational systems.
wrongs: The production network where student services are running.
A public computer lab used by any student during exams.
The original server left connected to the internet during testing.
why: Isolation reduces the risk of spreading malware or altering systems that are still in operation.
example: Malware from a seized image is opened only on a lab bench network that has no route to campus services.
scenario: A seized image may contain harmful software and must be reviewed without touching campus services. Where should that review happen?
scenarioWhy: An isolated analysis environment has no path to the live operational systems.

definition: A US federal test of whether expert evidence rests on methods that are tested, reviewed, and reliable.
wrongs: A rule that accepts any tool output without asking about its reliability.
A file-system feature that journals disk changes.
A hash comparison used only to verify an image copy.
why: Daubert focuses on the reliability of the method, including testing, peer review, and known error concerns.
example: Before expert testimony, the court asks whether the lab's imaging method has been tested and whether its error rate is known.
scenario: A US federal court asks whether an examiner's method is tested, reviewed, and reliable enough for expert testimony. Which standard is that?
scenarioWrongs: A rule that all tool output is automatically accepted
scenarioWhy: The Daubert standard is the federal reliability test applied to expert methods and testimony.

definition: Preparing systems in advance so useful and trustworthy evidence can be preserved when an incident occurs.
wrongs: Waiting until after logs are gone to decide whether logging was needed.
Deleting time sources so clocks cannot be compared.
Avoiding backups because they might contain records.
why: Readiness includes logging, time synchronization, and retention choices made before an incident.
example: A department enables centralized logs and synchronized clocks months before any investigation is needed.
scenario: A department wants useful logs and reliable clocks already in place before any incident. What preparation is that?
scenarioWrongs: Turning logs on only after they have been deleted
scenarioWhy: Forensic readiness is advance preparation so evidence can be preserved when an incident happens.

definition: The unwanted mixing of data from one case, device, or action with a different item of evidence.
wrongs: The deliberate separation of each case onto its own sterile media.
The use of a new seal for each evidence bag.
The storing of unrelated cases in separately labeled containers.
why: Mixing remnants from another case can make later findings unreliable and hard to explain.
example: A destination drive still contained files from an older case, so those files appeared beside the new image.
scenario: Files from an older case appear on the drive used for a new image because the drive was not wiped. What problem occurred?
scenarioWrongs: A successful hash match of one image
scenarioWhy: Cross-contamination is the mixing of leftover data from one case into another item of evidence.

definition: Computing two different cryptographic hashes of the same evidence so both can be checked for a match.
wrongs: Hashing two unrelated cases and expecting their digests to match.
Using one short checksum that is not meant to detect intentional changes.
Storing the evidence hash only in human memory.
why: Agreement of two independent hashes, such as MD5 and SHA-256, strengthens the integrity check of the copy.
example: The acquisition log records both an MD5 and a SHA-256 digest of the same drive image, and both match at verification.
scenario: The lab wants two independent digests of one image, such as MD5 and SHA-256, recorded together. What practice is that?
scenarioWrongs: Hashing two different cases against each other
Keeping the digest only in memory
Using a one-digit sum as the only check
scenarioWhy: Dual hashing computes two different cryptographic hashes over the same evidence.
